1. Carbohydrate classification, D-aldoses, epimers and anomers

Monosaccharides are commonly polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. The broader carbohydrate family includes compounds that give such units on hydrolysis. A single sugar unit cannot be hydrolysed to a simpler carbohydrate. Oligosaccharides contain a small number of monosaccharide residues and polysaccharides contain many. A carbonyl at C1 defines a typical aldose. A carbonyl at C2 is usual for a ketose. Glucose is an aldohexose, fructose a ketohexose and ribose an aldopentose.

Recognising a carbohydrate

Many sugars fit the empirical pattern Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ. Their defining chemistry is that they are polyhydroxy aldehydes, polyhydroxy ketones, or compounds that furnish such units on hydrolysis. Acetic acid fits an empirical hydrate pattern but falls outside this definition. Deoxy sugars show why the formula is only a historical guide. Glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone illustrate the smallest aldose and ketose.

Fischer projections of selected D-ketoses

D-RibuloseD-XyluloseD-Allulose (D-psicose)D-FructoseD-SorboseD-Tagatose

Classification by hydrolysis

Raffinose is a trisaccharide. Hydrolysis yields D-galactose, D-glucose and D-fructose. Its galactose attaches α(1→6) to the glucose unit of sucrose. A ketose commonly has one fewer stereocentre than the corresponding open-chain aldose with the same carbon count.

Raffinose hydrolysis

The α-galactosyl residue is attached to C6 of the glucose residue of sucrose.

D-aldoses in Fischer projection

In a Fischer projection, horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away. Place the chain with the most oxidised end at the top. The OH at the stereocentre farthest from the carbonyl determines D/L: right for D and left for L. The table records OH positions from the highest stereocentre downward. In an open-chain aldohexose there are four stereocentres, so there are 16 stereoisomers in total and eight in the D series.

GET RAXL groups glyceraldehyde (G), erythrose and threose (ET), and ribose, arabinose, xylose and lyxose (RAXL).

All Altruists Gladly Make Gum In Gallon Tanks gives allose, altrose, glucose, mannose, gulose, idose, galactose and talose.

Read OH positions from C2 down. In each pair the first child has C2 OH on the right and the second has it on the left. Both inherit the lower pattern from their parent and keep the lowest stereocentre in the D configuration.

Epimers and anomers

Here R and L refer to right and left on the drawing. Enantiomers reverse every stereocentre. Epimers differ at exactly one stereocentre. D-Mannose is the C2 epimer of D-glucose and D-galactose is its C4 epimer. Anomers differ at the anomeric carbon created by ring closure.

Are D-glucose and D-fructose epimers?

They have the same molecular formula but differ in carbonyl connectivity. They are constitutional isomers.

2. Reactions of glucose and fructose

Preparation of D-glucose

Sucrose gives equimolar glucose and fructose. Complete starch hydrolysis consumes one water per glycosidic linkage. The usual repeating-unit equation is (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ + nH₂O → nC₆H₁₂O₆.

Glucose and fructose reactions with structures

1. Exhaustive reduction

Retention of the six-carbon chain establishes an unbranched carbon skeleton.

2. Acetylation of all five OH groups

Ac = CH₃CO. Ac₂O releases AcOH and AcCl releases HCl formally. The cyclic acetates carry OAc at the anomeric carbon. Separate α and β glucopyranose pentaacetates are possible.

3. Carbonyl reduction to alditols

Reduction of glucose introduces no new stereocentre. Reduction of fructose creates C2 stereochemistry and gives two epimeric alditols.

4. Bromine water

Glucose and fructose are distinguished under the usual bromine-water test conditions.

5. Hydroxylamine gives oximes

Oxime C=N geometry may give E/Z forms. The sugar stereocentres outside the carbonyl group are retained.

6. Alkaline silver and copper reagents

Write carboxylate under alkaline conditions and the free acid after acidification. The ketose first equilibrates with aldoses. Balanced test equations are given with the diagnostic tests.

7. Nitric acid oxidation

The fructose products represent competing oxidation pathways. The plus signs list products found in the mixture and do not give a balanced single-molecule equation.

8. Cyanohydrin formation

Addition at the planar carbonyl creates a new stereocentre. Both configurations at that carbon are possible. The original sugar centres are unchanged.

9. Net osazone reaction

All three yield glucosazone because C1 and C2 become hydrazone functions and C3–C5 have the same configuration.

  1. What changes: C1 and C2 both become C=N–NHPh groups. C3, C4 and C5 keep their configurations.
  2. What the three equivalents do overall: two phenylhydrazine units remain in glucosazone. The net coproducts are one aniline, one ammonia and two waters for each hexose.
  3. How to read the mechanisms: the classical Fischer sequence is useful formal bookkeeping. Weygand A proposes rearrangement of the first phenylhydrazone with aniline loss and a monoimino α-dicarbonyl intermediate. Nitrogen-labelling work supports A for the studied labelled D-fructose derivative. Scheme B is shown as a historical alternative.
  4. Prediction rule: compare the C3–C5 Fischer rows in this hexose set. Ignore the initial configuration at C2 and whether the starting carbonyl is at C1 or C2.

Fischer’s classical formal scheme

This classical sequence balances the overall reaction. It is a formal treatment of the oxidation rather than a demonstrated elementary pathway.

Weygand proposal A

The initial phenylhydrazone rearranges and expels aniline. The imine nitrogen is then lost as ammonia during conversion to the osazone. Nitrogen-labelling studies support this route for studied derivatives, including a D-fructose derivative.

Weygand proposal B

This panel records the alternative historical proposal at the level of connectivity. The proposed fragmentation releases aniline. The third equivalent of phenylhydrazine replaces the remaining imine function, with ammonia as the nitrogen-containing by-product. These intermediates are historical hypotheses.

10. Dehydration and rehydration in hot acid

  1. Dehydration. The hexose loses three waters to give 5-(hydroxymethyl)furfural, HMF. Fructose also gives HMF under acidic conditions.
  2. Rehydration and ring cleavage. HMF consumes two waters to give a five-carbon levulinic acid molecule and a one-carbon formic acid molecule.
  3. Net: C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₅H₈O₃ + HCOOH + H₂O. Competing condensation can produce humins.

11. Alcoholic fermentation

  1. Glycolysis supplies two pyruvate molecules per glucose.
  2. Decarboxylation removes C1 of each pyruvate as CO₂.
  3. Reduction converts acetaldehyde C=O into CH₂OH and regenerates NAD⁺ for glycolysis.

12. Action of dilute and concentrated alkali

R is the unchanged C3–C6 chain. The related enediolate is present under alkaline conditions. Strong alkali gives a mixture of products.

13. Action of alkaline-earth hydroxides

  1. Classroom observation. The soluble calcium–glucose product is traditionally called calcium glucosate. “Glucosate” here does not denote oxidation at C1.
  2. Structure. In an alkaline solution, oxygen donors from the sugar can bind Ca²⁺. The reaction scheme records association and does not assign a unique binding site or stoichiometry.
  3. Distinction. Calcium gluconate contains the carboxylate of gluconic acid. Forming a calcium–glucose complex is not the oxidation that produces gluconate.

14. Dehydration and charring

The equation is the idealised dehydration limit. The black residue from actual charring is a mixture of carbonaceous material.

3. Uses of glucose, modified sugars, practice and sweetness

Uses of glucose

Glucose applications. Glucose is used in confectionery, fruit preserves, fermentation and silvering. Its reduction product sorbitol is an intermediate in some industrial vitamin C routes. Calcium gluconate is made from the oxidised glucose derivative and is chemically distinct from calcium glucosate.

Monosaccharides in glycoconjugates

N-Acetyl-D-glucosamineN-Acetyl-D-galactosamineN-Acetyl-D-neuraminic acid

Glucose, galactose, mannose, xylose, fucose and the three N-acetyl sugars illustrated here occur in glycoconjugates. These structures are building blocks in human glycobiology. Their occurrence does not make all eight essential dietary nutrients.

  1. Answer: A, B and E. The C3–C5 pattern is left, right, right for D-glucose, D-fructose and D-mannose.
  2. C (D-galactose) differs at C4, D (L-sorbose) at C5 and F (D-allose) at C3.

  1. Answer: A–H, J and K. The aldoses open to aldehydes. D-fructose gives aldoses in alkaline solution. Lactose and maltose each have one free anomeric centre.
  2. I is sucrose, whose two anomeric carbons are bonded. L shows the amylose component of starch. Starch and cellulose have very few reducing ends per unit mass and are conventionally scored negative in the usual qualitative test.

3. Which one change preserves the glucosazone structure: inversion at C2, C3, C4 or C5 of D-glucose?

Answer: C2. The epimer is D-mannose. The new C2 hydrazone has no tetrahedral C2 stereocentre.

4. For one mole of glucosazone, how many moles of phenylhydrazine are consumed and how many are incorporated?

Answer: Three are consumed and two are incorporated. The net coproducts are PhNH₂, NH₃ and two H₂O.

5. Predict the tests for D-fructose with bromine water and with Tollens reagent.

Answer: Negative with mild bromine water, positive with alkaline Tollens reagent after isomerisation.

Deoxy sugars and recognition by cell-surface glycans

L-Rhamnose is 6-deoxy-L-mannose. L-Fucose is 6-deoxy-L-galactose. Replacing the C6 hydroxymethyl group with methyl leaves the remaining stereocentres in place.

Glycoproteins carry glycans on proteins, and glycolipids carry glycans on lipids. At the cell surface, small differences at a glycan’s exposed end can determine whether a recognition protein binds it.

Carbohydrate-derived antibiotic. Streptomycin contains streptidine, streptose and N-methyl-L-glucosamine. It interferes with bacterial protein synthesis. Its carbohydrate-derived units illustrate how different ring substituents can be combined in one natural product.

4. Glucose stereochemistry, cyclic structures and mutarotation

D-glucose and its L enantiomer

D-GlucoseL-GlucoseL-Fucose (6-deoxy-L-galactose)

D/L is a configuration label. The L enantiomer of D-(+)-glucose is L-(−)-glucose under identical conditions. Inverting C5 alone changes the D/L series but gives a diastereomer, since the other stereocentres do not invert. The optical rotation of a diastereomer cannot be assigned from its Fischer projection.

Evidence from test responses and anomers

  1. Schiff reagent. Glucose does not give the usual rapid Schiff response expected of a simple aldehyde in the textbook test.
  2. Bisulfite. Glucose does not give the usual isolated sodium hydrogensulfite addition product under the textbook test conditions.
  3. 2,4-DNP. The classroom notes record no ordinary rapid hydrazone test under their conditions. Timing and acidity matter. This observation alone cannot establish the absence of the open-chain form.
  4. Hydroxylamine. Free glucose forms an oxime through its open-chain fraction. Glucose pentaacetate does not give the usual oxime because the anomeric hydroxyl is acetylated and ordinary ring opening is blocked.
  5. Reducing tests. Free glucose reduces Tollens, Fehling and Benedict reagents as the open-chain fraction is replenished.
  6. Two anomers. α and β glucose differ at C1. Their solutions approach the same optical rotation by mutarotation. Acetylation can give distinct α and β pentaacetates.
ObservationStructural inference
Formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and formation of n-hexane on prolonged reduction with HISupports an unbranched six-carbon skeleton

Oxidation with bromine water to gluconic acidThe accessible carbonyl is an aldehyde
Acetic anhydride gives a pentaacetateFive hydroxyl groups are available for acetylation in the cyclic form
Nitric acid gives glucaric (saccharic) acidOxidation converts both the aldehyde end and terminal primary alcohol into carboxyl groups
Glucose pentaacetate gives no oxime in the usual testAcetylation traps an anomeric derivative that lacks a free hemiacetal OH

When the aldehyde tests differ

Under usual test conditions free glucose reduces Tollens, Fehling and Benedict reagents. Glucose pentaacetate has its anomeric OH esterified, which blocks ordinary ring–chain interconversion.

Haworth projection and chair forms

  1. Make the ring. O5 attacks C1 of open-chain D-glucose. O5 becomes ring oxygen and the original carbonyl oxygen becomes the anomeric OH.
  2. Transfer the Fischer pattern. With ring oxygen at the upper right and C1 at the right, the C2 OH points down, C3 up and C4 down. D-glucose has C5–CH₂OH up.
  3. Assign the anomer. At C1, OH down and trans to C5–CH₂OH gives α. OH up and cis gives β.
  4. Convert to the ⁴C₁ chair. Keep each substituent up or down. Only α has axial C1–OH. The C2–C4 hydroxyls and C5–CH₂OH are equatorial in both anomers.

The C5 hydroxyl oxygen attacks the C1 carbonyl intramolecularly. Proton transfer gives a six-membered hemiacetal containing five carbons and one oxygen. The incoming oxygen becomes the ring oxygen. The carbonyl oxygen becomes the anomeric OH. This creates α- and β-D-glucopyranose, which can interconvert through the small open-chain population.

In the conventional Haworth drawing for D-glucose, put C1 at the right and the C5–CH₂OH group above the ring. Fischer OH groups on the right at C2–C4 point down in Haworth, giving down, up, down. α has its anomeric OH trans to C5–CH₂OH. β has it cis. For an L sugar the reference substituent is down in the analogous drawing.

Compare the ⁴C₁ chairs

Glucose and mannose in the ⁴C₁ chair

Keep the ring oxygen at the upper right. In the standard D-sugar Haworth orientation, a Fischer OH on the right projects down and one on the left projects up. Transfer those faces to the chair before deciding whether each group is axial or equatorial. A ring flip preserves up and down. Mutarotation changes the configuration at C1.

β-D-Glucopyranose places every non-hydrogen substituent equatorial in ⁴C₁. D-Mannose is the C2 epimer, so its C2–OH is axial in the same chair. The α form of D-mannose is favoured in its aqueous equilibrium. The anomeric effect is one contribution, alongside solvation and interactions between substituents.

Worked rotation example. For a glucose sample with [α] = +52.7°, use +112.2° for α and +18.7° for β. The α mole fraction is (52.7 − 18.7)/(112.2 − 18.7) = 0.364. The two-anomer approximation gives about 36% α and 64% β.

In the β anomer all five major substituents are equatorial. In the α anomer the C1 hydroxyl is axial while the other four major substituents remain equatorial.

Cyclic fructose

  1. Fischer projection. D-fructose has C2=O. Its C3, C4 and C5 OH groups are left, right and right.
  2. Five-membered ring. The C5 hydroxyl attacks C2. The ring is O5–C2–C3–C4–C5. C1 and C6 are exocyclic CH₂OH groups.
  3. Six-membered ring. The C6 hydroxyl attacks C2. The ring is O6–C2–C3–C4–C5–C6. C1 remains exocyclic and the C5 hydroxyl remains present.
  4. Anomeric centre. C2 is anomeric in both ring sizes. In the D-fructofuranose Haworth orientation shown, α has its C2 OH down and β has it up.

Open-chain D-fructose is CH₂OH–CO–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CH₂OH, with Fischer OH positions LRR at C3–C5. The anomeric carbon is C2. Attack by the C5 oxygen gives a five-membered fructofuranose hemiketal. Attack by the C6 oxygen gives a six-membered fructopyranose hemiketal. Both ring sizes occur in solution. Sucrose contains a β-D-fructofuranosyl residue.

The four cyclic D-fructose forms

Fructose ring sizes in solution

Fructose can close through O5 or O6. Typical aqueous measurements show β-fructopyranose as the major form, with appreciable β-fructofuranose. A representative distribution is about 2% α-pyranose, 66% β-pyranose, 7% α-furanose and 25% β-furanose. The fractions vary with conditions. Sucrose contains β-D-fructofuranose, even though β-D-fructopyranose predominates for free fructose.

  1. Positive: A, B, D, H and K. A and B are two projections of the same free glucose anomer. H opens to an aldehyde. D gives an α-hydroxyketone that can isomerise under the test conditions. K has a free glucose C1.
  2. Negative: C, E, F, G, I and J. C and E have locked anomeric acetal or ketal centres. F and G do not give an aldehyde or an aldose-forming α-hydroxyketone on opening. I carries three oxygen substituents at the marked ring carbon. J is sucrose and both anomeric centres are linked.

Mutarotation

In water, freshly dissolved α-D-glucose has a specific rotation near +112° and β-D-glucose near +19°. Both approach about +52.7° at equilibrium under standard textbook conditions. Treating these as the only two forms gives xβ ≈ (112 − 52.7)/(112 − 19) ≈ 0.64. In the preferred 4C1 chair of β-D-glucopyranose all five non-hydrogen substituents are equatorial. The α anomer has an axial OH at C1. The anomeric effect can favour axial electronegative substituents in some glycosides, depending on solvent and structure. A common orbital explanation is donation from a ring-oxygen lone pair into an antiperiplanar σ* orbital of the C1–X bond. In aqueous glucose, the β anomer is more abundant.

For D-glucose use approximately +112° for α, +18.7° for β and +52.7° after equilibration. If α is the only other appreciable form, its mole fraction is (52.7 − 18.7)/(112 − 18.7) ≈ 0.364. β therefore accounts for about 64%. A formal count of four acyclic stereocentres gives 16 aldohexoses. For a fixed glucopyranose ring connectivity, including both anomeric configurations doubles that count. D-glucose itself has two pyranose anomers.

5. Glycosidic linkage and glycoside formation

An alcohol can convert a free anomeric hemiacetal into a glycoside under acid catalysis. Water leaves after protonation, followed by alcohol attack and deprotonation. The anomeric OH is replaced by OR. The resulting acetal or ketal cannot enter ordinary ring–chain equilibrium without cleavage of its glycosidic bond. A free anomeric OH at another residue can still make the entire molecule reducing.

Anomeric OH and OMe

Acid-catalysed glycoside formation and hydrolysis

Protonate the anomeric OH, then lose water to give an oxocarbenium-like intermediate stabilised by ring oxygen. Alcohol attacks either accessible face, followed by deprotonation. Only the anomeric OH is replaced in ordinary glycoside formation.

Track the anomeric carbon during methyl glucoside formation

Why an axial glycoside can be favoured

In the axial glycoside geometry, a ring-oxygen lone pair can donate into the antibonding orbital of the anomeric C1–O bond. This stereoelectronic stabilisation can favour the axial glycoside despite its steric cost. Solvent and substituents also affect the equilibrium. In water, free D-glucose still has predominantly the β glucopyranose anomer.

4,6-O-Benzylidene protection

O4 and O6 both bond to the benzaldehyde-derived CH(Ph) carbon. The anomeric OMe remains axial.

Acetals can select different glucose forms

  1. Glucopyranose. The 4,6-O-benzylidene product has a six-membered acetal ring fused trans to the glucose chair. The stable chair pair places phenyl equatorial in the acetal ring.
  2. Glucofuranose. Acid-catalysed acetonide formation favours five-membered acetals. Glucose can give the 1,2:5,6-diacetonide, with a cis-fused 1,2-acetonide and a second acetonide on the side chain.
  3. Open-chain glucose. The aldehyde can be trapped by two equivalents of a thiol as a dithioacetal. C1 bears H and two SR groups, so it cannot serve as a free aldehyde while protected.

O-, S- and N-glycosides

Compare the atom directly bonded to the anomeric carbon. An O-glycoside has C–O–R, a thioglycoside has C–S–R, and a nucleoside has C–N to the heterocyclic base. In forming an O-glycoside, protonation converts the anomeric OH into a good leaving group. Departure of water gives a resonance-stabilised glucosyl electrophile. Alcohol addition and deprotonation complete the substitution.

α-D-Galactopyranose has cis hydroxyl pairs at C1/C2 and C3/C4. Acetone under acid catalysis can protect both pairs, leaving C6 available for selective chemistry. The geometry of a diol governs whether it can form a cyclic acetal readily.

Exhaustive methylation followed by aqueous acid hydrolysis yields 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl-D-glucose. Acid cleaves the anomeric acetal, while the ordinary methyl ethers survive. In the open-chain product C5 bears the unmethylated hydroxyl because its oxygen was the pyranose ring oxygen. This distinguishes C5 closure from C4 closure.

Natural glycoside example. Salicin is the β-D-glucopyranoside of salicyl alcohol at its phenolic oxygen. Hydrolysis gives D-glucose and 2-(hydroxymethyl)phenol.

6. Disaccharides, cellulose, starch and glycogen

Sucrose

Glcp and Galp are pyranose residues. Fruf is a fructofuranose residue. Locate C1 in an aldose and C2 in fructose before deciding whether a sugar is reducing. Sucrose occupies both anomeric positions, so it gives neither an ordinary reducing test nor mutarotation before hydrolysis. On hydrolysis the mixture becomes levorotatory because fructose’s negative rotation outweighs glucose’s positive rotation. This is inversion of sucrose.

Sucrose hydrolysis

Maltose

A wavy bond at the free C1 indicates an unspecified anomeric configuration. Maltose, cellobiose and lactose can interconvert between α and β at that end. In sucrose the linkage joins α-D-glucose C1 to β-D-fructose C2. The fructose ring is turned to face the glucose ring, so the β linkage and fructose C5–CH₂OH both point down in this drawing.

Maltose hydrolysis

How the α(1→4) linkage in maltose is established

Oxidise the reducing end first

Br₂/H₂O gives maltobionic acid (maltose’s reducing end becomes gluconic acid).
Exhaustive methylation with (CH₃)₂SO₄/OH⁻ gives the methyl ester and O-methyl ethers.
Acid hydrolysis cleaves the glycosidic bond and hydrolyses the methyl ester.

Protect the reducing end as a methyl glycoside first

Use CH₃OH/H⁺, then (CH₃)₂SO₄/OH⁻.
Acid hydrolysis removes the anomeric acetal groups.

In both routes the acceptor’s C4 was occupied by the glycosidic bond during methylation. Hydrolysis therefore exposes a free C4 OH. The methylation pattern identifies the linkage position. Assignment of the donor’s α configuration requires separate stereochemical evidence.

In classical methylation analysis, exhaustively methylate free OH groups, hydrolyse glycosidic bonds, and identify the partially methylated monosaccharides. A linkage position is exposed after hydrolysis. Interpret the ring-oxygen position separately because it was also unavailable for methylation. For a terminal Glcp residue the usual product is 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methylglucose. A 4-linked Glcp residue gives 2,3,6-tri-O-methylglucose, and a 4,6-linked branch residue gives 2,3-di-O-methylglucose. This method identifies attachment positions. Anomeric configuration needs other evidence.

What linkage does 3,4,6-tri-O-methylglucose indicate for a Glcp residue?

C2 was occupied during methylation, so the residue was substituted at O2.

Lactose

Lactose hydrolysis

Hydrolysis of a methyl glucoside

1. Protonation

Protonate the methoxy oxygen bound to C1. The resulting –O⁺HCH₃ group can leave as methanol.

2. Loss of methanol

The C1–OCH₃ bond breaks. The ring oxygen stabilises the glucosyl oxocarbenium intermediate by resonance.

3. Addition of water

Water attacks C1 from either face. Deprotonation yields α- and β-D-glucopyranose. The free anomeric hydroxyl permits mutarotation in solution.

Cellobiose

Cellobiose hydrolysis

Uronic acids: oxidation at C6

Glucuronic and galacturonic acids have CO₂H in place of the C6 CH₂OH group. They retain the C1 aldehyde in their open-chain forms and can close to hemiacetals.

Cellulose and its derivatives

Cellulose segment · β(1→4)

Esterification of cellulose

The repeating unit has three available hydroxyls, at C2, C3 and C6. Exhaustive substitution gives cellulose trinitrate or cellulose triacetate.

Cellulose xanthate and regeneration

Acid treatment regenerates cellulose as fibres through a spinneret for viscose rayon, or as a sheet through a slit for cellophane. Glycerol is used to plasticise the films.

Starch and amylose

Amylose segment · α(1→4)

Starch–iodine colour

This is a noncovalent inclusion complex. Heating can weaken the colour and cooling can restore it.

Amylopectin

Amylopectin branch · α(1→4) backbone and α(1→6) branch

By mass, typical starch contains about 15–20% amylose and 80–85% amylopectin, with variation by source. The α(1→4) chain of amylose can wind into a helix. Glycogen has the same linkage types as amylopectin and has more frequent branches. Cellulose is an unbranched β(1→4) glucan.

Glycogen

Glycogen is the principal storage polysaccharide in animals. Like amylopectin, it has α(1→4) chains and α(1→6) branches. Its branches are more frequent.

For an acyclic assembly from n glucose units, there are n − 1 glycosidic bonds, even if branched. Its exact composition is C6nH10n+2O5n+1. The repeating-unit formula is (C₆H₁₀O₅)n. A typical connected glucan tree has one reducing end. Each additional branch point with one extra outgoing chain adds one nonreducing end.

A glycogen fragment has 12 residues and three branch points, each with one extra chain. Count the links and terminal ends.

It has 11 links, one reducing end and four nonreducing ends.

Deducing glycosidic linkages from methylation

Tag the free hydroxyls with methyl groups, then cleave the glycosidic bonds. A hydroxyl uncovered at a nonanomeric position marks a former linkage site after accounting for the ring oxygen. The methylation pattern gives the position. Enzyme specificity or independent stereochemical evidence establishes α or β.

SugarLinkageReducing behaviour
IsomaltoseGlc-α(1→6)-GlcFree C1 on the second glucose
MelibioseGal-α(1→6)-GlcFree C1 on the glucose
Trehaloseα-D-Glcp-(1↔1)-α-D-GlcpBoth anomeric carbons are linked
StachyoseGal-α(1→6)-Gal-α(1→6)-Glc-α(1↔2)-β-FruAll anomeric carbons are linked

Worked deduction. A reducing Glc–Glc disaccharide yields 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methylglucose and 2,3,4-tri-O-methylglucose after methylation and hydrolysis. C6 of the second residue was occupied. If an α-glucosidase cleaves the linkage, the structure is isomaltose.

Cyclodextrins. α-, β- and γ-cyclodextrin contain six, seven and eight α(1→4)-linked glucose residues, respectively. They have no reducing end. A repeating 2,3,6-tri-O-methylglucose fragment, together with the absence of a reducing end, is consistent with a cyclic α(1→4) chain.

7. Sugar-chain shortening, extension and carbonyl interconversion

Wohl and Ruff degradation

Wohl degradation

The shown methoxy/acylal route records the course variant schematically. The essential transformation is elimination of the original aldehyde carbon as cyanide, then deprotection to D-arabinose. Silver-assisted cyanide removal is also used in variants.

Ruff degradation

Original glucose C1 leaves as CO₂. C2 becomes the new aldehyde carbon. The peroxide/iron step is represented as a net oxidative decarboxylation.

Kiliani–Fischer chain extension

Kiliani–Fischer chain extension

The nitrile carbon becomes C1 of the new aldose. The carbonyl of the starting pentose becomes C2.

Aldose–ketose interconversion

Aldose to ketose through the osone

Selective reduction of glucosone’s C1 aldehyde leaves the C2 ketone intact.

Ketose to aldose through alditol and lactone

or

Here R denotes the C5–C6 side chain, –CH(OH)–CH₂OH. The product series depends on the separated alditol and the end oxidised. Uncontrolled nitric acid oxidation can continue to the aldaric acid. An aldono-1,4-lactone forms when the C4 OH esterifies the C1 acid.

Fischer’s configurational proof of D-glucose

Start with the eight D-aldohexose Fischer patterns. In the shorthand below, R and L specify the side of each OH from C2 downward. They indicate positions in a projection, rather than CIP descriptors.

  1. Oxidation gives an optically active aldaric acid. Reject D-allose (RRRR) and D-galactose (RLLR), whose equivalent ends make their aldaric acids meso.
  2. Chain shortening gives an optically active-on-oxidation D-aldopentose. The compatible retained patterns are LRR and LLR, corresponding to D-arabinose and D-lyxose. Chain extension of LLR would also give D-galactose, which contradicts the active aldaric acids obtained from both C2 epimers. Therefore the common pentose has the LRR pattern.
  3. Adding a stereocentre above LRR gives RLRR or LLRR. Interchanging CHO and CH₂OH and rotating the Fischer projection by 180° reverses the order and exchanges left with right. LLRR maps to itself, identifying mannose. RLRR gives a different sugar, L-gulose, identifying glucose.

8. Barfoed, Molisch and Seliwanoff tests

Barfoed test

Reducing monosaccharides give a rapid red Cu₂O precipitate. Fructose can also give a positive result. Longer heating can lead to disaccharide positives, so reaction time matters.

Molisch test

The dehydrated sugar reacts with α-naphthol. The bis(naphthol) formula shows the conventional condensation connectivity. The colour indicates a family of conjugated products rather than one universal isolated dye.

Seliwanoff’s test

Ketohexoses form HMF rapidly. Aldoses can colour more slowly. Sucrose can become positive after hydrolysis releases fructose.

An unknown gives a rapid Seliwanoff response and a positive Tollens test before hydrolysis. What likely explains both?

A free ketohexose such as fructose reacts rapidly in Seliwanoff’s test and isomerises in the alkaline Tollens reagent.

Laboratory tests for carbohydrates: procedure, theory and results

Aim. To study the characteristics of carbohydrates, fats and proteins in pure form and to detect them in foodstuffs.

Classes. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes, polyhydroxy ketones or compounds that give these on hydrolysis. Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further; oligosaccharides give 2–10 monosaccharide units (disaccharides give two); polysaccharides give a large number. A monosaccharide with an –CHO group is an aldose and one with a keto group is a ketose. Carbohydrates that taste sweet are sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose); sugars are reducing or non-reducing, detected by Fehling’s, Benedict’s and Tollens’ tests. Prepare 1 % stock solutions of glucose, fructose and sucrose and divide each among test tubes A, B, C, D.

TestReagent and theoryProcedureResult and inference
Molisch’s (all carbohydrates)Conc. H₂SO₄ hydrolyses glycosidic bonds to monosaccharides and dehydrates them to furfural (hydroxymethylfurfural for hexoses), which condenses with 1-naphthol to an unstable deep-violet product. Some other organic compounds also respond. 1-Naphthol is highly destructive to tissues in high concentration.2–3 drops of 1 % alcoholic 1-naphthol in tube A; pour 2 mL conc. H₂SO₄ down the side so that it forms a separate layer at the bottom.Purple ring at the junction of the two layers: carbohydrate present.
Fehling’sFehling’s A (CuSO₄) + Fehling’s B (alkaline Na-K tartrate). Tartrate complexes Cu²⁺ so it stays dissolved in alkali and Cu(OH)₂ does not precipitate (the free [Cu²⁺] stays below the solubility product). Reducing sugar: RCHO + 2 Cu²⁺ + 5 OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + Cu₂O↓ + 3 H₂O.Mix 1 mL each of A and B, add to tube B, heat in a water bath.Orange-red Cu₂O precipitate (sometimes first yellow CuOH): reducing sugar. Glucose and maltose positive; sucrose gives no reaction.
Benedict’sAlkaline CuSO₄ with sodium citrate (citrate complexes Cu²⁺) and Na₂CO₃ as the base. D-glucose + Cu²⁺(citrate) → D-gluconic acid + Cu₂O.1 mL Benedict’s reagent in tube C; boil in a water bath for 2 min.Orange-red precipitate: reducing sugar.
Tollens’Ammoniacal AgNO₃: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 2 OH⁻ → 2 Ag + RCOONH₄ + H₂O + 3 NH₃.Add NaOH dropwise to 1 mL AgNO₃ to get Ag₂O, dissolve it in NH₄OH, add the reagent to the sugar and warm on a water bath. Never heat on a direct flame (explosion hazard).Silver mirror on the tube wall: reducing sugar.
Barfoed’s (monosaccharide vs disaccharide)Cupric acetate in acetic acid: weakly acidic, reduced only by monosaccharides within about 5 min; RCHO + 2 Cu²⁺ → RCOOH + Cu₂O (brick-red, less dense, so brick-red rather than orange-red). Disaccharides react more slowly because the aldehyde is masked in the acetal linkage; prolonged boiling hydrolyses them and gives a false positive.10 drops of 1 % sugar + 1 mL Barfoed’s reagent; boil in a water bath for 5 min.Brick-red precipitate: monosaccharide. Disaccharides do not give it.
Test for sucroseSucrose is non-reducing; acid hydrolysis frees glucose and fructose.5 drops conc. HCl to 5 mL of 1 % sucrose, heat in boiling water, cool, neutralise with NaOH to slightly alkaline; repeat the reducing-sugar and Seliwanoff tests.Now positive in Fehling’s/Benedict’s/Tollens’ and Seliwanoff’s tests (fructose is present).
Seliwanoff’s (ketose vs aldose)Ketoses dehydrate rapidly in acid to furfurals that give a coloured product with resorcinol (1,3-dihydroxybenzene). Aldoses form furfural slowly (β-elimination is needed first), so avoid prolonged heating.2 mL Seliwanoff’s reagent + 10 drops of 1 % sugar; heat in boiling water for 2 min.Ketohexose (fructose): red. Ketopentose: blue-green. Aldoses: no colour within 2 min.
Iodine test (starch)Starch + I₂ forms the blue starch–iodine inclusion complex.Suspend 0.5 g starch in 5 mL water, pour into 50 mL boiling water to get a colloid; add a few drops of aqueous iodine.Blue colour: starch present (wheat, rice, maize, potato).

All monosaccharides are reducing sugars. Disaccharides with a free hemi-acetal group (for example maltose and lactose) are mild reducing sugars; sucrose is the exception. The Fehling/Benedict reaction can be used quantitatively to estimate reducing sugar in blood and urine.

Discussion questions with answers

How will you distinguish between sucrose and glucose?

Glucose is a reducing sugar and gives an orange-red precipitate with Fehling’s or Benedict’s solution and a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent; sucrose has no free anomeric –OH or carbonyl and gives no reaction. After acid hydrolysis, sucrose also gives positive tests (because it gives glucose and fructose), and unlike glucose it then gives Seliwanoff’s colour.

Why does fructose reduce Fehling’s solution and Tollens’ reagent although it has a ketone group?

In alkaline medium fructose, an α-hydroxy ketone, tautomerises through an enediol to glucose and mannose (Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein transformation), and the aldoses formed are oxidised.

What is the role of tartrate and citrate ions in Fehling’s reagent and Benedict’s reagent?

They form soluble complexes with Cu²⁺ in alkaline medium and release Cu²⁺ in very low concentration, so the solubility product of Cu(OH)₂ is never reached and the Cu(OH)₂ does not precipitate.

Precautions. Use fresh reagents and only the required amounts; never heat the Tollens’ test tube over a direct flame; avoid prolonged boiling in Barfoed’s and Seliwanoff’s tests.

Monosaccharide reaction summary

ReactionProduct or inference
NaBH₄ reductionD-Glucose gives D-glucitol (sorbitol). D-Fructose gives glucitol and mannitol because C2 becomes stereogenic.
Bromine waterAn aldose gives an aldonic acid under the mild conditions. Fructose lacks an aldehyde and is negative in the standard comparison.
Nitric acid oxidationD-Glucose gives glucaric acid. Track oxidation at both ends of the aldose chain.

Ruff degradationOxidise to an aldonic acid, then oxidatively decarboxylate. Original C2 becomes the new C1. Both D-glucose and D-mannose give D-arabinose.
Wohl degradationForm the aldoxime, dehydrate to the nitrile during acetylation, then remove the terminal carbon as cyanide on treatment with base. The aldose loses one carbon.

Fehling, Benedict and Tollens tests

Fehling uses tartrate and Benedict uses citrate. A free aldose hemiacetal can open to an aldehyde. A free fructose hemiketal opens to a ketose that isomerises under alkaline test conditions. A generic ketal or hemiketal is not automatically Tollens-positive.

Further JEE reactions

Periodate oxidation of D-glucose

Exhaustive oxidation gives five molecules of formic acid and one molecule of formaldehyde per molecule of D-glucose. Use the open-chain form to track the six carbons. The cyclic and open-chain forms interconvert in water.

5 HIO₄⟶
H–C(=O)–H + 5 H–C(=O)–OH + 5 HIO₃

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 5 HIO₄ → HCHO + 5 HCOOH + 5 HIO₃

  1. Hydration converts the C1 aldehyde to –CH(OH)₂. An oxygen at C1 and the C2 hydroxyl oxygen bind the same iodine(VII) centre to give a five-membered cyclic periodate ester.
  2. The ester fragments. The C1–C2 bond breaks as the two C=O bonds form and iodine(VII) is reduced to iodine(V). C1 gives formic acid and the C2 end of the remaining chain becomes an aldehyde.
  3. Repeat the hydrate–ester–cleavage sequence along the chain. C1 through C5 give HCOOH. Terminal C6 starts as –CH₂OH and gives HCHO in the last cleavage.

Wolfrom homologation of D-arabinose to D-fructose

In this example an aldopentose becomes a ketohexose. The original aldehyde carbon becomes C2 of the ketose. The added carbon becomes C1.

Br₂ / H₂O⟶
Ac₂O, then SOCl₂⟶
R–C(=O)–Cl
CH₂N₂⟶
R–C(=O)–CH=N⁺=N⁻
R–C(=O)–CH=N⁺=N⁻
Aqueous AcOH, then ester hydrolysis⟶
  1. Oxidation and protection. Oxidise C1 to CO₂H, protect the alcohols as acetates, then replace the carboxylic OH by Cl to give the protected acyl chloride. R denotes the protected three-stereocentre chain with terminal CH₂OAc.
  2. Carbon–carbon bond formation. The carbon end of the diazomethane resonance form ⁻CH₂–N⁺≡N attacks the acyl carbon. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate expels Cl⁻. Deprotonation gives the α-diazoketone, R–C(=O)–CH=N⁺=N⁻.
  3. Replace the diazo group and remove the protecting groups. Protonation at the diazo carbon makes N₂ a leaving group. Water or acetate captures that carbon as N₂ departs. Hydrolysis removes the acetate esters and gives R′–C(=O)–CH₂OH, with the original Fischer stereocentres retained in R′. The ketone remains at the old aldehyde carbon.

Predicting periodate fragments and aldaric-acid symmetry

A suitable pair of oxygenated neighbours can bind periodate in a cyclic intermediate. In a flexible chain, an internal CHOH that is cleaved at both sides gives HCOOH. A terminal CH₂OH gives HCHO. A ketone carbon flanked by cleavable hydroxyl-bearing carbons gives CO₂ under exhaustive cleavage.

SubstrateHIO₄ consumedCarbon-containing products
Glycerol2 equivalents2 HCHO + HCOOH
D-Glucose5 equivalentsHCHO + 5 HCOOH
D-Fructose5 equivalents2 HCHO + 3 HCOOH + CO₂

Optical-activity check. Oxidising both ends of D-galactose gives meso galactaric acid. Reducing the aldehyde instead gives meso galactitol. In both products the end groups are identical, so the RLLR arrangement in the Fischer projection can accommodate an internal plane of symmetry. Reducing D-xylose gives xylitol.

Practice with structures, mechanisms and linkage evidence

  1. Identify the axial groups in β-D-mannopyranose and α-D-mannopyranose, both drawn as ⁴C₁ chairs.

    The C2 hydroxyl is axial in both. The C1 hydroxyl is axial only in α; it is equatorial in β.

  2. A solution contains 40% α-D-glucose and 60% β-D-glucose. Estimate its specific rotation using +112.2° and +18.7°.

    0.40(112.2) + 0.60(18.7) = +56.1°. Both anomers contribute a positive rotation.

  3. Exhaustive methylation followed by aqueous acid gives an open-chain sugar with a free hydroxyl at C4 and a methyl ether at C5. Which oxygen closed the original ring?

    O4 was the ring oxygen. Closure between C1 and O4 made a five-membered furanose.

  4. A reducing hexose is either glucose or fructose. Both consume five equivalents of periodate. What measurement identifies fructose?

    Exhaustive oxidation of fructose gives CO₂ and two equivalents of HCHO. Glucose gives no CO₂ and gives one equivalent of HCHO.

  5. A disaccharide releases galactose and glucose. Its methylated glucose fragment retains OMe at C2, C3 and C4 only, and an α-galactosidase cleaves it. Identify the linkage.

    Gal-α(1→6)-Glc. C6 is uncovered after cleavage, and the donor anomeric configuration is α. The sugar is melibiose.

  6. A nonreducing Glc–Glc disaccharide gives two identical 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl fragments. What linkage follows from these data? What information is still needed?

    Both C1 atoms are linked, so the linkage is 1↔1. The methylation result leaves the configuration at each C1 undetermined.

  7. Two D-hexoses have Fischer OH patterns RLRR and LLRR. Which returns to the same structure after true end-group interchange?

    LLRR does. Reversing the sequence and exchanging R and L gives LLRR again. RLRR gives LLRL.

  8. You want to remove an O-acetyl group while retaining a methyl glycoside. Choose the type of hydrolysis and explain.

    Base-promoted ester cleavage removes the acetate. An ordinary methyl glycoside is an acetal and is stable under these basic conditions.

  9. Both C2 and C3 carry OH on a methyl ribofuranoside. What happens to that periodate cleavage site after replacing C2–OH with H?

    The C2–C3 vicinal diol is removed. The corresponding oxidative cleavage is unavailable in the 2-deoxy derivative.

  10. A nonreducing glucose oligomer gives only 2,3,6-tri-O-methylglucose after linkage analysis. Why is a cyclic structure plausible?

    Each residue is substituted at C4 and has a linked C1. A closed α(1→4) chain accounts for the absence of terminal or reducing residues, if the α configuration is established separately.

10. Amino acids and their side chains

For JEE Advanced, prioritise amino acids, peptide linkage, primary and secondary protein structure, fibrous and globular proteins, and the chemical composition and structure of DNA and RNA. The detailed tests, synthesis, tertiary and quaternary structures, and hormones extend that core for textbook study.

The α-carbon lies next to the carboxyl carbon. An α-amino acid has its amino group on this carbon. Draw its neutral skeleton as H₂N–CH(R)–COOH and its dipolar form as ⁺H₃N–CH(R)–COO⁻. In proline the side chain closes back onto nitrogen, so the neutral molecule contains a secondary amine.

In the usual Fischer projection put COOH at the top and R at the bottom. NH₂ on the left gives the L series. Glycine is achiral. Most standard L-amino acids are S at Cα, while L-cysteine is R because the sulfur-bearing side chain has higher CIP priority than the carboxyl group. L-Thr and L-Ile also have a stereocentre in the side chain. D/L describes configuration. The sign of optical rotation is measured experimentally.

Side-chain classAmino acidsR groups or identifying feature

AromaticPhe, Tyr, TrpBenzyl, p-hydroxybenzyl, indol-3-ylmethyl
Polar uncharged near neutral pHSer, Thr, Cys, Asn, GlnCH₂OH, CH(OH)CH₃, CH₂SH, CH₂CONH₂, CH₂CH₂CONH₂
AcidicAsp, GluCH₂COOH, CH₂CH₂COOH
BasicLys, Arg, His(CH₂)₄NH₂, (CH₂)₃NH–C(=NH)–NH₂, imidazolylmethyl

The three-letter names are glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, proline, methionine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine, glutamine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, lysine, arginine and histidine. For adult human nutrition, the essential set is His, Ile, Leu, Lys, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp and Val. Nutritional classification is independent of side-chain charge.

Fischer structures of the standard amino acids

Ph denotes phenyl. The Fischer structures show the α-centre and explicitly show the side-chain configuration of L-isoleucine (2S,3S) and L-threonine (2S,3R).

Classification by position and by side chain

α: HOOC–CH(NH₂)–R　•　β: HOOC–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–R　•　γ: HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–R

Count away from the carboxyl carbon. The first carbon is α. Protein backbones use α-amino acid residues. Glycine has two hydrogens at Cα and is achiral. Proline’s α-nitrogen belongs to a five-membered ring and is a secondary amine in the free amino acid. L and D describe relative configuration. Most protein L-amino acids are S at Cα; L-cysteine is R by CIP priority.

Side-chain familyMembers and how to recognise them
Nonpolar aliphaticGly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro and Met. GAVLI groups Gly (R = H) with the alkyl examples.
AromaticPhe, Tyr and Trp in the usual biochemical grouping. Histidine’s imidazole is also chemically aromatic, and His is commonly grouped with basic amino acids.
Hydroxyl-bearingSer and Thr have alcoholic OH; Tyr has a phenolic OH.
Sulfur-bearingCys has a thiol and Met has a thioether. Cysteine thiols can form a disulfide.
Acidic and amide pairsAsp/Glu have an extra carboxyl group. Asn/Gln have corresponding side-chain amides.
BasicHis, Arg and Lys. Read the imidazole, guanidinium and terminal amino groups respectively.

Essential in the standard adult list: His, Ile, Leu, Lys, Met, Phe, Thr, Trp and Val. Arginine is conditionally essential. The mnemonic that includes Arg is useful only with that distinction.

Amino acid families, mnemonics and the 20 standard amino acids

Amino acids contain both an amine (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid (–COOH) group. By the position of the amino group: α: NH₂–CH(R)–COOH, β: NH₂–CH₂–CH(R)–COOH, γ: NH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH(R)–COOH. Proteins are built from α-amino acids.

11. Zwitterions, pI and electrophoresis

A zwitterion has formal charges of both signs and zero net charge. The isoelectric point, pI, is the pH at which the population has zero average net charge. Below pI the average charge is positive and the species migrates toward the cathode. Above pI it is negative and migrates toward the anode.

Write the dominant charge sequence by removing one proton at a time in order of pKₐ. For a simple amino acid, H₂A⁺ ⇌ HA ⇌ A⁻. At pI, [H₂A⁺] = [A⁻]. Multiplying the two acid-dissociation expressions gives K₁K₂ = [H⁺]² at this condition, so pI = (pK₁ + pK₂)/2. For a side-chain ionisation, average the two pKₐ values bracketing the zero-charge species in the standard exam approximation. Minor charge states can give small corrections to this approximation.

ExampleApproximate pKₐ values in ascending orderCharge sequenceApproximate pI
Gly2.34, 9.60+1 → 0 → −15.97
Asp1.88, 3.65, 9.60+1 → 0 → −1 → −22.77
His1.82, 6.00, 9.17+2 → +1 → 0 → −17.59
Lys2.18, 8.95, 10.53+2 → +1 → 0 → −19.74

At pH 6.00, which way do Asp and Lys move?

Asp is above its pI and moves toward the positive anode. Lys is below its pI and moves toward the negative cathode.

Select the two pKₐ values around the neutral species

Start at low pH with the groups protonated. Remove one proton at a time in rising pKₐ order. Find the species with net charge zero and average the pKₐ values for entering and leaving it.

ExampleSuccessive chargesIllustrative pKₐ valuespI calculation
Alanine+1 → 0 → −12.34, 9.69(2.34 + 9.69)/2 ≈ 6.02
Lysine+2 → +1 → 0 → −12.18, 8.95, 10.53(8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74
Glutamic acid+1 → 0 → −1 → −22.19, 4.25, 9.67(2.19 + 4.25)/2 = 3.22

For a simple ampholyte, multiply Kₐ₁ = [H⁺][HA]/[H₂A⁺] and Kₐ₂ = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. At pI, the +1 and −1 populations are equal, so [H⁺]² = Kₐ₁Kₐ₂. The definition of pI is zero mean net charge. Solubility is often relatively low near pI, although precipitation depends on conditions.

Paper electrophoresis at pH 5. Asp migrates toward the anode. Ala and Arg migrate toward the cathode. Ala has only a small mean positive charge near its pI. Exact migration distances also depend on mobility and experimental conditions.

Behaviour at pH 7, isoelectric point and solubility

  • Basic amino acids are cationic at pH 7. To reach the isoelectric point add OH⁻ (a base) to remove H⁺ from the side-chain ammonium group: the net charge goes from +1 to 0, at pH > 7.
  • Acidic amino acids are anionic at pH 7. To reach the isoelectric point add some H⁺: the side-chain carboxylate is protonated, net charge −1 → 0, at pH < 7.
  • Isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which the maximum concentration of the amino acid exists as the zwitterion (dipolar ion).
  • At the pI there is no electrophoresis: the molecule shows no net migration towards the anode or cathode.
  • At the pI the dipolar-ion concentration is highest and the amino acid has its lowest solubility (it is easiest to precipitate). Making the solution more acidic or more basic increases the concentration of a more soluble ion and the solubility rises.
  • An amino acid with more –COOH than –NH₂ groups has pI < 7; one with more –NH₂ than –COOH has pI > 7.

Derivation of pI for a simple amino acid

  1. H₂N⁺-form (cation, C⁺) ⇌ zwitterion (Z.I.) + H⁺, with Ka₁ = [Z.I.][H⁺]/[C⁺]
  2. zwitterion ⇌ anion (A⁻) + H⁺, with Ka₂ = [A⁻][H⁺]/[Z.I.]
  3. at the pI, [A⁻] = [C⁺]; multiplying: Ka₁·Ka₂ = [H⁺]² (take –log)
  4. pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2
  5. Equivalent route with Kb: for the neutral form N, N ⇌ A⁻ + H⁺ (Ka) and N + H₂O ⇌ C⁺ + OH⁻ (Kb). At the pI, [A⁻] = [C⁺] gives [H⁺]² = Ka·Kw/Kb, so pI = ½(pKa + pKw − pKb) = ½(pKa + 14 − pKb)
Amino acidpKa values usedNeutral species lies betweenpI
Alanine2.34 (–COOH), 9.6 (–NH₃⁺)pKa₁ and pKa₂(2.34 + 9.6)/2 = 5.97
Lysine2.18 (–COOH), 8.95 (α-NH₃⁺), 10.79 (ε-NH₃⁺)the two amino pKa values(8.95 + 10.79)/2 = 9.87
Glutamic acid2.19 (α-COOH), 4.25 (side-chain COOH), 9.67 (–NH₃⁺)the two carboxyl pKa values(2.19 + 4.25)/2 = 3.22

Another textbook set uses pKa 10.53 for the lysine side chain, which gives pI = 9.74. Both values are acceptable if you use the pKa values given in the question.

How will you separate a ternary mixture of arginine, alanine and aspartic acid?

Spot the mixture on the middle of a filter paper soaked in a buffer of pH 5 and apply an electric field. Arginine (pI ≈ 10.8) and alanine (pI ≈ 6.0) have pI > pH, so they carry a positive charge and move to the cathode; aspartic acid (pI ≈ 2.8 < pH) is negative and moves to the anode. Alanine, only slightly positive at pH 5, moves slowly, while arginine moves fast, so the three separate.

12. Preparing and reacting amino acids

Functional-group reactions

The amine can be protonated, acylated, or protected. Nitrous acid converts a typical primary α-amino acid to the corresponding α-hydroxy acid with release of N₂. Detailed stereochemistry depends on the substrate and conditions. Acids can form esters with alcohol under acidic conditions, and activated carboxyl derivatives can form amides. In formol titration, reaction with formaldehyde suppresses the contribution of the amino group to the acid–base equilibrium, enabling titration under the prescribed conditions.

Heating and ring size

Typical textbook pathways include intermolecular condensation of two α-amino acid molecules to a six-membered 2,5-diketopiperazine, and elimination of NH₃ from suitable β-amino acids to form an α,β-unsaturated acid. γ- and δ-amino acids can cyclise to five- and six-membered lactams respectively. An ε-amino acid can give a seven-membered lactam under suitable conditions, as in the caprolactam framework. Count the carboxyl carbon and nitrogen in every lactam ring.

Which aldehyde gives valine by Strecker synthesis?

Valine has R = isopropyl. Use (CH₃)₂CHCHO, 2-methylpropanal. The aldehyde carbon becomes Cα.

Five-, six- and seven-membered lactams

Tracing atoms in the reaction schemes

For R–CHO, ammonia first forms an imine through a carbinolamine and loss of water. Protonation gives the iminium shown. Cyanide adds through carbon, producing R–CH(NH₂)–C≡N. Hydrolysis changes –C≡N to –COOH. The original aldehyde carbon is Cα; the cyanide carbon is the new carboxyl carbon. Without a chiral influence, addition to a planar imine or iminium that creates a stereocentre generally produces a racemate.

Follow the corresponding reductions. Hydrogenating the C≡N of cyanoacetic acid converts its nitrile carbon to –CH₂NH₂ and gives β-alanine. Reducing the –NO₂ group of nitroacetic acid gives glycine without changing the carbon count. In the Sørensen route the nitrogen is unmasked by phthalimide hydrolysis and one carboxyl group is lost during aminomalonic acid decarboxylation.

Heating check. Two glycines can lose two waters to give cyclo(Gly–Gly), a 2,5-diketopiperazine. A suitable β-amino acid can eliminate NH₃ to make an α,β-unsaturated acid. For H₂N–(CH₂)ₘ–COOH, intramolecular amidation gives a lactam with m + 2 ring atoms: 5, 6 and 7 for m = 3, 4 and 5.

13. Peptide bonds and protein structure

A peptide bond is the amide linkage –C(=O)–NH– between residues, with substituted amide nitrogen possible for proline. Write peptide sequences from N-terminus to C-terminus. A linear chain of n residues has n − 1 backbone peptide bonds. Relative to the free amino acids, its molecular formula is lower by (n − 1)H₂O. An unbranched head-to-tail cyclic peptide has n bonds and loses n H₂O in the same bookkeeping.

For directed coupling, protect the N-terminus of the future first residue and the carboxyl group of the future second residue. Activate the first residue’s free carboxyl group. The second residue attacks through its free amino group. Then remove the protecting groups as required. Reactive side chains may also need protection. Boc and Fmoc are common N-protecting groups. The amide nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character. The peptide unit is approximately planar and is usually trans.

Structural levelWhat to identify
PrimaryResidue sequence from N to C, with covalent linkage positions when specified
SecondaryLocal α-helices and β-sheets stabilised largely by backbone hydrogen bonding
TertiaryThe overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide chain
QuaternaryArrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits

In an α-helix the C=O of residue i hydrogen-bonds to the N–H of residue i + 4. β-sheets can be parallel or antiparallel. Hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ion pairs and disulfide links help stabilise folds. Two cysteine thiols can oxidise to a cystine disulfide. Fibrous proteins such as keratin serve mainly structural roles. Globular proteins include many enzymes and oxygen-binding proteins. Denaturation disrupts native folding and activity. Ordinary denaturation generally leaves the peptide backbone intact.

How many distinct linear tetrapeptides use two Gly, one Ala and one Val?

There are 4!/2! = 12 sequences. N → C direction matters. Each has three peptide bonds.

Read a peptide from N terminus to C terminus

The carboxyl carbon of residue 1 joins the amino nitrogen of residue 2. The sequence Gly–Ala begins with glycine and ends with alanine. Complete hydrolysis releases the original amino acids. For a linear, unmodified peptide of n residues, formation of its n − 1 peptide bonds has the formal net loss of n − 1 waters.

Glutathione and the disulfide redox pair

Glutathione is γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine. Its first amide uses the side-chain carboxyl of glutamate. The cysteine side-chain thiol is the redox site. The glutamate α-carboxyl remains free.

HOOC–CH(NH₂)–CH₂–CH₂–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH₂SH)–C(=O)–NH–CH₂–COOH

  1. First sulfur oxidation: an activated thiol can form a sulfenic acid, GS–OH, while peroxide is reduced.
  2. Disulfide formation: a second thiol reacts with the sulfenic acid to give GS–SG and water. The overall equation consumes two glutathione molecules per peroxide.

Native structure and denaturation

  1. Primary. Read the amino acid sequence from the N terminus to the C terminus.
  2. Secondary. Backbone C=O and N–H groups hydrogen-bond in local patterns. An α-helix generally links residue i to i + 4. A β-sheet uses hydrogen bonds between neighbouring strands.
  3. Tertiary and quaternary. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional fold of one chain. Quaternary structure describes how multiple chains assemble.
  4. Denaturation. Heating egg white disrupts native folding and leads to aggregation. The coagulated matrix retains much of the water. This change does not require hydrolysis of the peptide backbone.
  5. Shape and function. Keratin illustrates fibrous structural proteins. Insulin and albumin illustrate folded globular proteins with different functions.

Worked peptide structures and bond counts

For ordered synthesis with repetition, two available amino acids give 2² = 4 dipeptides and 2³ = 8 tripeptides. Three available amino acids give 3² = 9 dipeptides. Gly alone gives one sequence of each length. When names specify exact residue counts, use permutations of that multiset instead.

The amide resonance contributors explain planarity and restricted rotation about C–N. Backbone folding occurs mainly through rotations about N–Cα (φ) and Cα–C(=O) (ψ). A peptide bond to proline has a substituted amide nitrogen and lacks a backbone N–H donor at that linkage.

Recognise 3.6₁₃. The common right-handed α-helix has approximately 3.6 residues per turn. The i→i+4 backbone hydrogen bond closes a 13-membered ring when the backbone path and H are counted. Side chains project outward. In a β-sheet, side chains alternate above and below each strand; dashed contacts join C=O and H–N on neighbouring strands.

Fibrous and globular examples. Hair keratin contains α-helical coiled coils; silk fibroin is rich in β-sheets. Albumin illustrates a compact globular fold. Reducing cystine links softens hair. After reshaping, oxidation forms disulfide links that help retain the new arrangement.

The peptide plane and the bonds that rotate

The peptide C–N bond shares electron density with the carbonyl. That partial double-bond character keeps the peptide unit approximately planar. The torsion ω is measured around C(=O)–N and is usually near 180° in the trans unit. The main backbone rotations are φ about N–Cα and ψ about Cα–C(=O). Connecting successive peptide planes through those rotations enables an α-helix or β-sheet. An X–Pro bond can show a larger cis population than most other peptide bonds.

Structure in the viewerWhat to track
Helix formationOne backbone stays continuous as its geometry coils. Inspect the i → i + 4 contacts near the helical end of the slider.
β-sheetH bonds run between strands. Follow the N and C labels to distinguish parallel and antiparallel strands.
CrambinRotate the experimental Cα trace to see how one chain packs its secondary structures into a tertiary fold.

Amide resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character (about 1.33 Å, between 1.47 Å for C–N and 1.27 Å for C=N), so rotation about it is restricted and the peptide unit is planar. The C=O of one residue hydrogen-bonds to the N–H four residues farther along; R groups extend outward. The tighter 3₁₀ helix has a 10-atom ring (3.0 residues per turn) and the wider π-helix is 4.4₁₆. All peptide dipoles point the same way, so the N-terminal end is partly δ⁺ and the C-terminal end partly δ⁻. Proline has no N–H donor and usually breaks a helix.

Interactions in protein structure. Peptide bond (covalent): primary structure. Backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds: secondary structure. Hydrogen bonds between side chains (–OH, –NH₂, –COOH, Trp N–H), ionic –COO⁻···⁺H₃N–, van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions of R groups, and disulphide –S–S– bridges: tertiary (and quaternary) structure. Disulphide bonds do not define an α-helix.

The free amino end is the N-terminal residue and the free carboxyl end the C-terminal residue: H₂N–(AA₁)–(AA₂)–(AA₃)–…–COOH. A polypeptide with more than about 100 residues and molecular mass above 10,000 is called a protein; the distinction is not sharp, and a smaller polypeptide with a well-defined conformation, such as insulin (51 residues), is also called a protein.

Draw the structure of Val–Glu and label the N- and C-terminal residues.

H₂N–CH[CH(CH₃)₂]–C(=O)–NH–CH(CH₂CH₂COOH)–COOH. Val is the N-terminal residue (free –NH₂) and Glu the C-terminal residue (free α-COOH; its side-chain –COOH is also free).

Fibrous and globular proteins

FibrousGlobular
StructurePolypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bonds, giving a fibre-like structureChains coil around to give a spherical shape
Solubility in waterInsolubleUsually soluble
RoleStructuralFunctional (enzymes, hormones, transport)
ExamplesKeratin (hair, wool, silk), myosin (muscle), collagenInsulin, albumin, haemoglobin, enzymes

Hair: α-keratin and the chemistry of a “permanent” wave

Hair is made of α-keratin, largely α-helix. Two α-helices wind round each other to form a supercoil; bundles of supercoils form a strand of hair. Disulphide (–S–S–) bridges between neighbouring chains hold the shape.

Tertiary structure, random coil and denaturation

Tertiary structure of a typical globular protein contains α-helical segments joined by stretches of random coil where the chain is folded. Secondary and tertiary structure are stabilised by hydrogen bonds, disulphide bonds, van der Waals forces and electrostatic attraction. Quaternary structure is the shape adopted when two or more polypeptide chains aggregate into one protein complex.

Denaturation. Because the tertiary structure of a globular protein is held by weak interactions, a modest change in temperature or pH can disrupt it. The primary structure stays intact; the folded chain becomes a randomly looped chain. Solubility drops sharply (egg white turns solid on cooking), biological activity is lost, and most enzymes stop working. Denaturation is usually irreversible; rare cases of spontaneous renaturation restore biological activity.

N terminus. Sanger labelling with FDNB followed by total hydrolysis identifies a DNP-labelled end group. A lysine side chain can also be labelled, so distinguish its derivative. In one Edman cycle, phenyl isothiocyanate tags the terminus; acid-assisted cyclisation releases the first residue, which is converted to a phenylthiohydantoin derivative. The shortened peptide remains available for the next cycle.

C terminus. Carboxypeptidases release accessible C-terminal residues. Early released products help identify that end; enzyme specificity and a blocked terminus can affect the result. Partial cleavage followed by fragment overlap can reconstruct a sequence.

Worked overlap. An N-terminal fragment is Gly–Ser–Lys and a second fragment is Ser–Lys–Ala. Their two-residue overlap gives Gly–Ser–Lys–Ala.

Terminal analysis and every protein test in full

N-terminal analysis: Sanger’s method

Acid hydrolysis breaks every peptide bond, so the whole peptide is destroyed; only the N-terminal residue is labelled.

Sequencing from the N-terminus: Edman degradation

Unlike Sanger’s method, Edman degradation leaves the rest of the chain intact, so the cycle can be repeated residue by residue.

C-terminal analysis and partial hydrolysis

Carboxypeptidases are exopeptidases (enzymes that cleave the peptide bond at the end of a chain). Carboxypeptidase A removes the C-terminal residue as long as it is not arginine or lysine, and carboxypeptidase B removes it only if it is arginine or lysine (in practice, proline at the C-terminus also resists A).

Once both terminal residues are known, the protein is hydrolysed with dilute acid (partial hydrolysis) to cleave only some peptide bonds. The fragments are separated, the composition and terminal residues of each are determined, and the original sequence is assembled by lining up the fragments where they overlap.

Laboratory tests for proteins and fats, and testing foodstuffs

Tests for proteins

Proteins are nitrogenous compounds built from amino acids (egg albumin, soya bean, pulses, fish, milk). Because of characteristic side chains, amino acids show typical colour reactions that proteins also show; proteins can be told apart from free amino acids by the biuret reaction and by coagulation.

Tests for oils and fats

Oils and fats are triglycerides: esters of glycerol with long-chain fatty acids. Triglycerides that are liquid at room temperature are oils (mostly of plant origin) and those that are solid are fats (mostly animal). If the three acyl groups are the same the triglyceride is simple; if they differ it is mixed. Many natural fatty acids contain two or three double bonds (polyunsaturated oils). Fats and oils are insoluble in water.

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins in foodstuffs

Take milk, wheat flour, rice flour, gram flour and legume powder. Use 0.5 mL of milk for each test. For the flours, boil 100 mg of the sample in 10 mL of distilled water to get a colloidal solution and run the tests on it.

15. Nucleosides, nucleotides and DNA/RNA

A nucleoside contains a base attached to the anomeric C1′ of a pentose. The β-N-glycosidic bond joins C1′ to N9 of a purine or N1 of a pyrimidine. A nucleotide is a phosphorylated nucleoside. AMP contains adenine, ribose and one phosphate. ATP has three phosphates. The phosphate nearest ribose forms an ester and neighbouring phosphate groups are joined by phosphoanhydride bonds.

FeatureDNARNA
Pentose2-Deoxy-D-ribose, with H at C2′D-Ribose, with OH at C2′
Standard purinesAdenine and guanineAdenine and guanine
Standard pyrimidinesCytosine and thymineCytosine and uracil
Usual architectureDouble-stranded, antiparallelOften single-stranded with local base-paired folds
Alkaline behaviourMore resistant to backbone cleavageThe 2′-OH can attack the adjacent phosphate, giving a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate intermediate

A phosphodiester linkage connects the 3′ oxygen of one sugar and the 5′ oxygen of the next sugar through a phosphate. A linear strand of n nucleotides has n − 1 such links. Two separate linear strands forming n base pairs have 2(n − 1) backbone links in total. In B-DNA the strands wrap into a right-handed helix. Hydrogen bonds account for pairing specificity and stacking interactions also help stabilise the structure.

For standard double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C in total, so total purines equal total pyrimidines. These equalities need not hold within an individual strand. If there are n base pairs and g are G–C, the total hydrogen-bond count is 2(n − g) + 3g = 2n + g. Heat can separate strands by disrupting noncovalent interactions. Complementary strands can anneal again under suitable conditions.

Replication copies DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA, and translation uses the mRNA sequence to assemble a polypeptide. mRNA carries the coding information, tRNA connects codons to amino acids and rRNA helps form the catalytic core of the ribosome.

A 300 bp duplex has 40% G+C. Find its H-bond count.

There are 120 G–C pairs and 180 A–T pairs. The count is 3 × 120 + 2 × 180 = 720.

Pentoses and nitrogenous bases

From nucleoside to dinucleotide

  1. N-glycosidic bond. C1′ of the sugar attaches to N9 of a purine or N1 of a pyrimidine.
  2. Base and sugar sets. DNA uses A, G, C and T with 2-deoxyribose. RNA uses A, G, C and U with ribose. Complete hydrolysis yields the pentose, bases and phosphoric acid.
  3. RNA in alkali. Base removes the proton from the 2′-OH. The resulting 2′-O⁻ attacks the neighbouring phosphate, forming a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate as the downstream 5′-O group leaves. Hydrolysis opens the cyclic phosphate. The analogous intramolecular pathway is unavailable to DNA because its sugar has H at C2′.
  4. Read the strand. Follow the covalent backbone from 5′ to 3′. Base pairing is noncovalent. A–T and G–C pairs align two strands in opposite directions.

Reading a nucleotide, a strand and a base pair

ObjectRecognise it byWorked example
NucleosideBase + sugar with one β-N-glycosidic bond at C1′.Thymine + 2-deoxyribose gives thymidine (deoxythymidine in this context).
NucleotideNucleoside with phosphate at a specified position.Thymidine 5′-monophosphate contains thymine, 2-deoxyribose and one phosphate.
Dinucleotide3′-O of one sugar and 5′-O of the next share phosphate.5′-ApG-3′ has adenosine on the 5′ side and guanosine on the 3′ side.
Base pairHydrogen bonds across opposite strands; the covalent backbone runs outside.A–T uses two canonical H bonds and G–C uses three. RNA uses A–U and G–C in a canonical stem.

Reverse complement. Given 5′-AGTC-3′, first align the partner as 3′-TCAG-5′. Written in its own 5′→3′ direction it is 5′-GACT-3′. The order changes as well as the bases.

RNA cleavage logic. Under base, an RNA 2′-oxygen can attack the neighbouring backbone phosphorus. Loss of the 5′-O group leaves a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate; subsequent hydrolysis can give 2′- and 3′-phosphates. A normal DNA residue lacks the attacking 2′-OH.

Three RNAs. mRNA supplies codons; tRNA presents an anticodon and carries an amino acid at its 3′-CCA end; rRNA is both scaffold and part of the catalytic centre of the ribosome. Local base pairing can fold a single RNA chain, as in a stem–loop. The structural models represent connectivity and selected geometry.

Read strand direction and follow one covalent link

From subunit to chain. An adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine or uracil ring is a base. Joining C1′ of the sugar to N9 of adenine or guanine, or to N1 of the pyrimidines, makes a nucleoside. Adding phosphate makes a nucleotide. A sequence written 5′ to 3′ follows covalent sugar–phosphate links. Hydrogen bonds align complementary strands and base stacking contributes to duplex stability.

Compare the models. Open the DNA crystal view to rotate an experimental sugar trace, then select the unwrapped view to read the base-pair pattern. In the strand-separation view, pairing contacts disappear while each backbone remains continuous. In RNA, compare a short stem–loop with the longer tRNA schematic, where the anticodon loop and the 3′-CCA amino-acid attachment end are on different arms.

Worked check. A linear duplex contains 100 base pairs and 56% of its bases are A or T in total. There are 56 A–T and 44 G–C pairs, giving 244 base-pair H bonds. The two covalent chains together contain 198 phosphodiester connections.

Nucleic acids: sugars, bases, base pairing and RNA types

A nucleic acid is a polynucleotide. A nucleoside = base + sugar. A nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphoric acid (phosphate). Nucleotides are joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds.

ComponentDNARNA

Purine bases (two rings)Adenine (A, 6-aminopurine), Guanine (G, 2-amino-6-oxopurine)Adenine, Guanine
Pyrimidine bases (one ring)Cytosine (C), Thymine (T, 5-methyluracil)Cytosine, Uracil (U)

16. Enzyme action and kinetics

An enzyme accelerates a reaction by lowering the activation barrier. It changes how quickly equilibrium is reached. The equilibrium constant and the reaction’s overall ΔG stay fixed at a given temperature. The active site binds the substrate and helps stabilise the transition state. In induced fit, binding and conformational adjustment are coupled. Some enzymes need a metal ion or an organic cofactor. The apoenzyme lacks the required cofactor and the holoenzyme is the complete form.

For a simple single-substrate enzyme under initial-rate Michaelis–Menten conditions, v₀ = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). At [S] = Km, the rate is half of Vmax. At high substrate concentration the active sites are mostly occupied and the rate approaches Vmax. An apparent Km is a kinetic parameter. Its relation to binding affinity depends on the mechanism.

Inhibition modelApparent KₘApparent Vₘₐₓ
CompetitiveIncreasesUnchanged
Pure noncompetitiveUnchangedDecreases
UncompetitiveDecreasesDecreases
MixedIncreases or decreasesDecreases
EnzymeReaction
Sucrase (invertase)Hydrolyses sucrose to glucose and fructose
Maltase / lactaseHydrolyse maltose / lactose respectively
AmylaseHydrolyses susceptible α(1→4) links in starch
UreaseHydrolyses urea, ultimately yielding ammonia and carbon dioxide in the simplified product equation
Catalase2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
Alcoholic fermentationA series of enzyme-catalysed reactions converts glucose to ethanol and CO₂ in yeast

How much substrate gives 80% of Vmax?

0.80 = [S]/(Kₘ + [S]), so [S] = 4Kₘ.

Substrate specificity and energy barriers

Maltase catalyses the hydrolysis of maltose to two glucose molecules. Sucrase catalyses sucrose hydrolysis. Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering the activation barrier. They do not change the free-energy difference between the same initial and final states.

Example: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P. Substrate binding precedes the chemical step, and the enzyme is released after product formation. At a fixed enzyme concentration, sufficient substrate can saturate the active sites.

A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble. B₁₂ is a useful exception to the idea that water-soluble vitamins have limited body stores. The reducing behaviour of vitamin C comes from its enediol group. It can be oxidised to dehydroascorbic acid.

Hormones are chemical signals. Insulin is a peptide hormone with two chains linked by disulfide bonds, while glucagon is a single-chain peptide. Cortisol and aldosterone are steroids derived from cholesterol. Adrenaline is a catecholamine and thyroxine is an iodinated tyrosine derivative.

Hormone classes and their roles

  1. Peptide hormones: insulin lowers and glucagon raises circulating glucose through opposing metabolic actions.
  2. Amino-acid derivatives: epinephrine and norepinephrine are catecholamines. Thyroxine is an iodinated tyrosine derivative.
  3. Steroid hormones: glucocorticoids regulate metabolic and stress responses. Mineralocorticoids regulate salt and water balance. Testosterone, estradiol and progesterone are steroid hormones.

Hormones as chemical messengers

Endocrine hormones travel in blood to target cells. The receiving cell must have a receptor able to recognise the messenger. The examples below are grouped by molecular skeleton.

Chemical classExamplesRole and structural clue
Peptides and proteinsInsulin, glucagon, growth hormone and endorphinsAmide-linked residues. Insulin lowers circulating glucose and glucagon raises it. Insulin has an A chain of 21 residues and a B chain of 30, two interchain disulfides and one A-chain disulfide.
Amino-acid derivativesEpinephrine, norepinephrine and thyroxineEpinephrine and norepinephrine have a catechol ring and a β-hydroxyamine side chain. Thyroxine (T₄) is a tyrosine-derived iodinated diaryl ether with four iodine atoms.
Adrenal cortex steroidsCortisol and aldosteroneCortisol is a glucocorticoid involved in metabolism and stress responses. Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid involved in water and salt balance.
Other steroidsTestosterone, estradiol and progesteroneTestosterone and estradiol participate in sexual development. Estradiol participates in menstrual-cycle regulation; progesterone helps prepare the endometrium for implantation.

Feedback example. After blood glucose rises, insulin signals glucose use and storage. When glucose falls, glucagon promotes release of glucose from the liver. Their opposing effects illustrate homeostasis.

Thyroid hormone synthesis requires iodine. Low thyroid hormone activity is called hypothyroidism; excess thyroid hormone activity is called hyperthyroidism. Adrenal insufficiency illustrates the importance of adrenal cortical hormones.

Recognise a peptide hormone by its connectivity

Solomons comparison. Oxytocin and vasopressin are nonapeptides with an intrachain disulfide. Human oxytocin and arginine vasopressin differ at residues 3 and 8. A peptide sequence can change recognition even when the two molecules have the same residue count and disulfide pattern.

Recognising hormones from a structure

Structural cueClassificationExamples and functions
Many backbone amides with linked amino-acid residuesPeptide or proteinInsulin and glucagon influence glucose homeostasis; growth hormone participates in growth regulation.
Catechol ring and amino-alcohol side chainTyrosine-derived catecholamineEpinephrine and norepinephrine participate in acute physiological responses.
Iodinated diaryl ether with an amino-acid side chainThyroid hormone derivativeThyroxine has four iodine atoms and helps regulate metabolism.
Three fused six-membered rings and one five-membered ringSteroidCortisol, aldosterone, estradiol, testosterone and progesterone share the steroid skeleton and differ in oxidation, substitution and unsaturation.

Vitamins: classification, sources and deficiency diseases

Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K (stored in liver and adipose tissue). Water-soluble vitamins: B-complex and C (excreted in urine and not stored, so they must be supplied regularly).

No.VitaminSourcesDeficiency diseases
1AFish liver oil, carrots, butter and milkXerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea of the eye); night blindness
2B₁ (thiamine)Yeast, milk, green vegetables and cerealsBeri-beri (loss of appetite, retarded growth)
3B₂ (riboflavin)Milk, egg white, liver, kidneyCheilosis (fissuring at corners of mouth and lips), digestive disorders and burning sensation of the skin
4B₆ (pyridoxine)Yeast, milk, egg yolk, cereals and gramsConvulsions
5B₁₂Meat, fish, egg and curdPernicious anaemia (RBC deficient in haemoglobin)
6C (ascorbic acid)Citrus fruits, amla and green leafy vegetablesScurvy (bleeding gums)
7DExposure to sunlight, fish and egg yolkRickets (bone deformities in children); osteomalacia (soft bones and joint pain in adults)
8EVegetable oils such as wheat germ oil, sunflower oilIncreased fragility of RBCs and muscular weakness
9KGreen leafy vegetablesIncreased blood clotting time
